Question five. Compare the materializations: view, table, incremental, ephemeral. Take the page's customer dimension: one row per customer, grouped from twenty-four events. As a view, only the query is stored, so every read regroups all twenty-four. It's cheap to build, slower to read, and always current: a new customer's event shows up at once. As a table, the result is computed once per run. A read is twelve stored rows, which is fast, but the table misses that new customer until the next run, and every run recomputes everything. Incremental keeps the table, and processes only new or changed rows on each run, for large tables that mostly append. And ephemeral isn't stored at all. Choose by read frequency, compute cost and data volume, not habit. An expensive model that dashboards read all day, from a source that changes nightly, should be a table. Question six. What is an ephemeral model, and when should you use it? dbt compiles it as a CTE, a common table expression, inside every model that refs it. Nothing is created in the warehouse. Use one for intermediate logic referenced once or twice. Referenced by many models, the same CTE is copied into each. And since it isn't a table, you can't query it or test it on its own.

Question seven. What is the difference between dbt run, dbt test, and dbt build? Run builds the models. Test runs the tests against models already built. Build does both, with seeds and snapshots too, in graph order: each model is tested as soon as it's built. The order is the point. With run, then test, a broken staging model has already fed everything downstream before any test fails. Build tests a model before anything downstream of it is built, so a failure stops where it starts. That's why build is the command to run in CI.
